<header class="dg-head dg-head-chapter"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 9</p><h1 class="dg-title">Newton-Cartan Theory</h1></header>
<div class="dg-motivation"><div class="dg-motivation-title">Motivation: Gravity as geometry: Newton’s theory on spacetime</div><div class="dg-motivation-upper"><p>In Newtonian mechanics, a particle of mass <span class="math inline">\(m\)</span>, described in Cartesian coordinates of an inertial frame, obeys  <span class="math display">\[
        m \, \ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t) = f^\alpha_\gamma(t) - m \, \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, \gamma_\mathcal{U}(t) \big),
        \qquad
        \sum_\alpha \partial_\alpha \partial_\alpha \Phi = 4 \pi G_N \, \rho ,
    \]</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(f^\alpha_\gamma\)</span> are the components of the forces acting on it and <span class="math inline">\(\Phi\)</span> is the gravitational potential, determined by the mass density <span class="math inline">\(\rho\)</span>. The gravitational term is unlike any other force: it is proportional to the very mass that measures inertia, so <span class="math inline">\(m\)</span> drops out of free fall, <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} = - \partial_\alpha \Phi\)</span>, and all bodies fall alike. The pseudo-forces of rotating or accelerated frames, such as the Coriolis and centrifugal forces, share this property, and they are not caused by any body: they are produced by the choice of frame. This suggests treating gravity not as a force, but as part of the geometry, as what “straight” means. On space this fails (Appendix <span class="dg-xref dg-xref-pending" data-label="section_Laplace_Question">B.21.4</span>), but on spacetime, the speed is part of the direction of the worldline, and the idea works.</p>
</div><div class="dg-motivation-lower">
<p><strong>Goal:</strong> reformulate Newtonian gravity on a 4-dimensional manifold, with gravity encoded in a connection.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Define a <strong>Newtonian spacetime</strong>: an <strong>absolute time</strong> <span class="math inline">\(t\)</span> and a torsion-free connection <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> along which time flows uniformly, with no notion of spatial distance.</p></li>
<li><p>Rephrase <strong>Newton’s axioms</strong>: free particles follow the autoparallels of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>, forces are measured as deviations from them, and absolute time is singled out as the parameter of every worldline.</p></li>
<li><p>In charts adapted to absolute time, identify the <strong>pseudo-forces</strong> (Coriolis, centrifugal, Euler, translational) with connection coefficient functions created by the chart alone.</p></li>
<li><p>Place <strong>gravity in the connection</strong>: uniform gravity is a pseudo-force, removed in a freely falling chart, whereas non-uniform gravity is curvature, which no chart removes. Poisson’s equation becomes a condition on the Ricci curvature, and the Riemann curvature measures the <strong>tidal acceleration</strong>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Already in Newton’s theory, gravity is the curvature of spacetime. General relativity (Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../gr/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_GR">10</a>) keeps this insight and replaces absolute time by a Lorentzian metric and time orientation.</p></div></div>
